# Using OR and RR to Derive Expected Proportions {#sec-or-rr-to-proportions}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Convert an expected RR into a second-group risk.
- Convert an OR without mistaking it for an RR.
:::

## The idea

Some reference studies provide a baseline outcome risk and an anticipated relative effect instead of two group probabilities. With a risk ratio $RR=p_2/p_1$, the planned group 2 risk is $p_2=RR\times p_1$. With an odds ratio, the conversion is nonlinear: $p_2=OR\,p_1/(1-p_1+OR\,p_1)$. The event definition, effect direction and transportability of baseline risk must remain consistent.

## When and how to apply it

Both transformations are planning conveniences. Estimates adjusted for covariates, marginal risks and conditional odds ratios may not be directly interchangeable. Check that the implied probability lies in [0,1] and that the reference effect is appropriate for the planned participants.

## Formula at a glance

$$
p_2=RR\,p_1 \qquad p_2=\frac{OR\,p_1}{1-p_1+OR\,p_1}
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
Suppose baseline event risk is 0.20 and planned RR is 1.5. The group 2 risk is $0.20\times1.5=0.30$. For OR 1.5, the group 2 risk is instead $0.2727$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Calculation logic

The example uses the stated planning assumptions and mathematical approximation. Explain why they apply before reporting the numerical result.

### Copy-and-run R

```r
p1 <- .20; rr <- 1.5; or <- 1.5
c(from_rr = rr*p1, from_or = or*p1/(1-p1+or*p1))
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
An OR of 2 does not generally mean that risk doubles.
:::

## Hands-on exercise

Repeat both conversions when the baseline risk is 0.05, 0.20 and 0.50, then comment on the divergence.

## Key message

Risk ratios and odds ratios imply different second-group probabilities except in special cases.
